parts.name: Central (Haversian) canals
parts.description: Central (Haversian) canal: the channel running along the axis of every osteon, about 50 µm across, lined by flattened bone-lining (endosteal) cells and osteoprogenitor cells. It carries one or two capillaries or postcapillary venules, unmyelinated nerve fibres and a little loose connective tissue, and is joined to neighbouring canals, the periosteum and the marrow by Volkmann canals. Canals enlarge and multiply in osteoporosis, and a resorption canal is the first stage of a new osteon. Eight representative osteons are shown. Dimensions and population density are selected for teaching visibility; this is not a morphometric specimen. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Haversian arterioles & capillaries
parts.description: Haversian arteriole/capillary: a thin vessel (derived mainly from the nutrient artery via the marrow, and from periosteal arteries in the outer cortex) supplying the osteon. Osteocytes up to ~100 µm away are fed by diffusion through canaliculi, which is why an osteon is only about 200 µm wide. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Haversian venules
parts.description: Haversian venule: a thin-walled postcapillary venule, usually wider than the arterial vessel beside it, draining through Volkmann canals to periosteal and medullary veins. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Haversian nerve fibres
parts.description: Nerve fibres of the central canal: mostly unmyelinated sympathetic (vasomotor) and sensory fibres running with the vessels; they contribute to bone pain and may regulate remodelling. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Concentric lamellae (set A)
parts.description: Concentric lamellae: 4–20 rings, each 3–7 µm thick, of mineralised type I collagen (with hydroxyapatite) laid down from the outside inwards around the central canal. Within one lamella the collagen fibres wind helically in a single direction; the pitch changes from one lamella to the next (a 'twisted plywood'), which is why alternate lamellae look light and dark in polarised light and why osteons resist bending and torsion. Sets A and B are the two alternating fibre orientations. Each visible band is an enlarged representative group of native lamellae, which are typically 4–6 micrometres thick in the cited human femoral sections. The display uses fewer bands so alternating fibre directions, the central canal and the six stepped disclosure levels remain distinguishable. Display band thickness is not a native lamellar measurement.

parts.name: Concentric lamellae (set B)
parts.description: Concentric lamellae: 4–20 rings, each 3–7 µm thick, of mineralised type I collagen (with hydroxyapatite) laid down from the outside inwards around the central canal. Within one lamella the collagen fibres wind helically in a single direction; the pitch changes from one lamella to the next (a 'twisted plywood'), which is why alternate lamellae look light and dark in polarised light and why osteons resist bending and torsion. Sets A and B are the two alternating fibre orientations. Each visible band is an enlarged representative group of native lamellae, which are typically 4–6 micrometres thick in the cited human femoral sections. The display uses fewer bands so alternating fibre directions, the central canal and the six stepped disclosure levels remain distinguishable. Display band thickness is not a native lamellar measurement.

parts.name: Cement lines
parts.description: Cement (reversal) line: a thin (1–5 µm), collagen-poor, mineral-rich, basophilic boundary around every osteon and interstitial fragment. It marks where osteoclasts stopped resorbing before osteoblasts began to fill the tunnel. Canaliculi rarely cross it, and microcracks are deflected along it, which toughens bone. A chaotic 'mosaic' of scalloped cement lines is the hallmark of Paget disease. The authored reversal boundary is 2 micrometres nominal at that scale.

parts.name: Lamellar collagen fibres (telescoped osteon)
parts.description: Collagen fibres of the lamellae: one osteon is drawn telescoped, like pulled-out tubes, to show that the collagen in each lamella winds helically round the canal and that the direction of the helix alternates between successive lamellae (Benninghoff's classic drawing).

parts.name: Osteocytes in lacunae
parts.description: Osteocytes in lacunae: former osteoblasts walled up in the matrix they made, lying in lens-shaped lacunae between the lamellae – oval and aligned round the canal in a transverse section, spindle-shaped along the osteon in a longitudinal one. They are ~90–95% of bone cells and live for years; they sense strain through fluid flow in the canaliculi and steer remodelling (sclerostin, RANKL) and phosphate balance (FGF23). Empty lacunae mean dead bone (osteonecrosis, sequestrum). Cells are sparsely sampled and enlarged 1.30 times for teaching, with smooth bodies and curved tapering dendrites. Representative transverse-face lacunae are real carved recesses around their osteocyte bodies. Other surface cells represent the distribution rather than a complete volumetric lacunar network.

parts.name: Canaliculi
parts.description: Canaliculi: fine channels (~0.5 µm) containing the dendritic processes of osteocytes, joined by gap junctions. They radiate from each lacuna across the lamellae towards the central canal and neighbouring lacunae, carrying nutrients, waste and signals – and normally stop at the cement line. Surface channels have enlarged hollow lumens surrounding finer osteocyte processes and common open junctions. The display lumen diameter is 1.04 micrometres; rat PXCT canaliculi near 0.15–0.17 micrometres are a comparative reference, not a human morphometric bound. Lacunar/canalicular porosity is not a complete volumetric network.

parts.name: Perforating (Volkmann) canals
parts.description: Perforating (Volkmann) canals: channels running transversely or obliquely through the cortex, linking central canals with one another and with the periosteal and endosteal (marrow) surfaces. Unlike central canals they have no concentric lamellae of their own – they simply cut across lamellae. On a transverse ground section they appear as channels joining neighbouring Haversian canals. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Volkmann canal vessels
parts.description: Vessels in the Volkmann canals: branches connecting the periosteal and medullary (nutrient) circulations with the capillaries of the central canals. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Volkmann canal venule
parts.description: Representative venous perforating course from a Haversian venule to the periosteal vein. Arterial and venous instructional colors identify separate circuits; no capillary bridge is authored between them. Colors are not literal blood appearance. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Interstitial lamellae
parts.description: Interstitial lamellae: angular fragments of older osteons (and of circumferential lamellae) left between intact osteons after remodelling partly resorbed them. Each is bounded by cement lines and cut across by the newer osteons around it. They are the oldest, most highly mineralised bone of the cortex and often contain empty lacunae.

parts.name: Outer circumferential lamellae
parts.description: Outer circumferential lamellae: several continuous lamellae running round the whole shaft beneath the periosteum, laid down by periosteal osteoblasts as the bone grows in width (appositional growth). Sharpey fibres anchor in them; osteons produced by remodelling gradually replace them from within.

parts.name: Inner circumferential lamellae
parts.description: Inner circumferential lamellae: thinner, less complete lamellae lining the marrow cavity, laid down by endosteal osteoblasts and interrupted where trabeculae join the cortex.

parts.name: Periosteum – cambium (osteogenic) layer
parts.description: Periosteum – cambium (osteogenic) layer: the inner, cellular layer applied to the bone, with osteoprogenitor (skeletal stem) cells, osteoblasts and a dense capillary network. Very active in children (growth in width) and after a fracture, when it forms the external callus – stripping the periosteum delays healing. Thin and inconspicuous in adults.

parts.name: Periosteum – fibrous layer
parts.description: Periosteum – fibrous layer: outer dense irregular connective tissue of type I collagen bundles and fibroblasts, carrying the periosteal vessels, lymphatics and a dense sensory innervation (so fractures, bone tumours and periostitis are painful). Tendons and ligaments blend into it; it is absent over articular cartilage.

parts.name: Sharpey fibres
parts.description: Sharpey (perforating) fibres: bundles of periosteal collagen that turn inwards and pierce the outer circumferential lamellae obliquely, anchoring the periosteum – and tendons and ligaments at their entheses – to the bone. The same fibres anchor the periodontal ligament in the tooth socket. Snug teaching recesses expose the insertion of complete closed collagen bundles. These recesses are an explanatory cut, not normal patent vascular canals or detached fibres.

parts.name: Periosteal artery
parts.description: Periosteal artery: part of the periosteal plexus that supplies roughly the outer third of the adult cortex through Volkmann canals (the inner two-thirds is supplied centrifugally by the nutrient artery). Periosteal flow is vital when the medullary supply is destroyed, e.g. after reaming for a nail. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Periosteal vein
parts.description: Periosteal vein: drains the outer cortex and periosteum; blood from most of the cortex leaves centrifugally through Volkmann canals to these veins. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Periosteal nerve
parts.description: Periosteal nerve: myelinated (Aδ) and unmyelinated (C) sensory fibres plus sympathetic fibres; the periosteum is the most pain-sensitive part of bone. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Endosteum
parts.description: Endosteum: a thin, discontinuous layer of flattened bone-lining cells, osteoprogenitor cells, osteoblasts and osteoclasts covering every inner bone surface – the endosteal surface of the cortex, the trabeculae and the lining of the canals. Its balance of resorption and formation sets the width of the marrow cavity, which widens with age as endosteal resorption wins.

parts.name: Osteoblasts
parts.description: Osteoblasts: plump cuboidal cells with basophilic (RNA-rich) cytoplasm, lined up on a surface where bone is forming over a thin seam of unmineralised osteoid. They secrete type I collagen, osteocalcin and alkaline phosphatase, control osteoclasts through RANKL and osteoprotegerin, and end as osteocytes, flat lining cells or by apoptosis. Driven by RUNX2 and Osterix.

parts.name: Bone-lining cells
parts.description: Bone-lining cells: flat, quiescent osteoblast-lineage cells covering inactive bone surfaces. They can be reactivated into osteoblasts, and retract to expose the surface to osteoclasts when remodelling starts.

parts.name: Osteoclasts (Howship lacunae)
parts.description: Osteoclasts: large multinucleated cells (fused monocyte–macrophage precursors, needing M-CSF and RANKL) sitting in resorption pits (Howship lacunae). A sealing zone (αvβ3 integrin) surrounds a ruffled border that pumps out H+ (carbonic anhydrase II, proton pump) to dissolve mineral and cathepsin K to digest collagen. Inhibited by bisphosphonates, denosumab (anti-RANKL) and calcitonin; defective in osteopetrosis.

parts.name: Osteoclast nuclei
parts.description: Five complete nuclei belong to each of three representative osteoclasts. Every nucleus is inside its own intact cell body. Hide osteoclast cytoplasm to disclose the nuclei; nuclear positions are a teaching sample, not a complete cell census.

parts.name: Trabeculae (spongy bone)
parts.description: Trabeculae (spongy, cancellous bone): a lattice of plates and rods of lamellar bone, each ~100–300 µm thick, usually without osteons – they are nourished from the marrow surface. Near the cortex they thicken and fuse into compact bone. They align with lines of stress (Wolff's law) and have a large surface, so they remodel fast and are lost first in osteoporosis (vertebral fractures).

parts.name: Red marrow
parts.description: Red (haematopoietic) marrow: sinusoids in a reticular-cell stroma packed with developing blood cells – erythroid islands, granulocyte precursors and megakaryocytes. In adults it remains in the axial skeleton and the proximal femur and humerus; the shafts of long bones turn to yellow, fatty marrow. Fat cells occupy carved spaces in the haematopoietic compartment and remain normally embedded; exposed portions are a teaching cut.

parts.name: Marrow adipocytes
parts.description: Marrow adipocytes: unilocular fat cells among the haematopoietic tissue. They increase with age (and after radiotherapy or in aplastic anaemia) until the marrow of the long-bone shafts is yellow.

parts.name: Nutrient artery branch
parts.description: Branch of the nutrient (medullary) artery: runs in the marrow cavity, supplies the marrow and, through endosteal branches entering Volkmann canals, the inner two-thirds of the cortex. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.

parts.name: Marrow sinusoid & central vein
parts.description: Marrow sinusoids and central venous sinus: wide, thin-walled vessels into which newly formed blood cells squeeze through the endothelium; they drain to the central sinus and nutrient vein. Source-authored section boundaries truncate some routes. These static sampled courses do not establish a complete connected circulation or continuous functional flow.
